body:
I think most coded implementation limits aren't tracking vectors, since they just identify the implementation, which was identifiable in lots of other easier ways. But if the implementation varies its limits based on characteristics of the user or their machine, or possibly if it avoids limits and just lets the renderer run out of memory or go to swap when it allocates too much, then the limits can become tracking vectors.

If we're going to put the big fingerprint on this paragraph, I think it needs a sentence or two about why a limit could be a tracking vector, and what a UA should do to avoid making its limits into tracking vectors.

This phrase, "should not enforce limits on unconstrained inputs", is strange. Unconstrained is another way of saying without limits.

I think you need to be clearer about what sorts of cases we're talking about. Here's an attempt:

> Many inputs to algorithms and APIs specified by documents using the Infra Standard are specified without limits on their size, resource usage, or similar. This style of specification is encouraged. It allows for competition among user agents, and allows the possibility of future computing environments to meet future computing needs.
>
> Nevertheless, user agents may impose ...

and then add a couple examples. (In addition to the useful additions Jeffrey suggests.) My attempts at examples:

> An API that allows creating an in-memory bitmap might be specified to allow any dimensions, or any dimensions up to some large limit like JavaScript's `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. However, implementations can choose to impose some implementation-defined (and thus not specified) limit on the dimensions, instead of attempting to allocate huge amounts of memory.

> A programming language specified on top of the Infra Standard might not have any maximum call stack size specified. However, implementations could choose to impose one for practical reasons.

body:
SGTM too.  Implementations need to determine how they allocate the resources necessary and so are free to set limits.

What would be really good is a little more about how specific limits are either dictated by implementation choices (which don't generally vary between installations of the same implementation and so don't contribute much to tracking), by hardware (which can vary and are consequently a source of tracking information), or both (with variable effect on tracking).  Implementations are might in a position to limit how much information is revealed through limits, such as through quantization.  This might involve sacrificing some potential performance as the applied limits might be smaller than what hardware is capable of, which puts the privacy goal in tension with any desire to maximize performance.  Again, this is an area of implementation differentiation as different approaches seek different trade-offs.

(In protocol land, there are often resource allocations that are made by others or jointly made, in which case this loose sort of approach doesn't work, but that applies on a case-by-case basis and probably isn't worth expounding upon.)
